doc.title: Al Vollmer interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, June 8, 2017

title: New Orleans revival, the Commodore Music Shop and New York clubs
summary: Rowe asks about the early-50s Dixieland revival; Vollmer recalls Bill Russell, the Commodore Music Shop, and going to Condon's, Jimmy Ryan's and Nick's.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Okay. This might have been after you left Hamilton but there was a short lived renewed interest in Dixieland and hot music. Do you recall when that — I believe it was in the early to mid-50s.

Yeah. Well that’s when the stuff was coming out of New Orleans. And there was that revival. Look magazine went down there and filmed, and of course the dean of them all was Bill Russell and his American music. And there were other people who were — I’ve forgotten his name now but he had the Icon label. So there was a renaissance. And of course actually there was the Commodore Music Shop. Now I went to the Commodore Music Shop when they were on the downtown side of 42nd Street. Later on that building was gutted and a new thing went up and the Commodore Music Shop moved across the street. But I remember hanging out there and listening to records. And so Bill Grauer and those people, they were part of it, they were the fundamental start.

And Eddie Condon. Now there was Condon’s and there was Jimmy Ryan’s. When I came in ’48, or ’47 actually, the original Ryan’s was there and Eddie Condon’s was there and Nick’s was there. So I went to all of those places.
